subject: Biology
name: Biology, Units 3 and 4
about: VCE, DNA, biochemistry, immunity and evolution
syllabus: VCE Biology Study Design (from 2022), Units 3 and 4

units.title: Unit 3: How do cells maintain life?

points.title: The structure of DNA and RNA
points.brief: Nucleic acids are chains of nucleotides. DNA is double-stranded with thymine; RNA is single-stranded with uracil.

points.title: The genetic code
points.brief: The code is read in triplets, is the same in almost all living things, and has more than one triplet for most amino acids.

points.title: Gene structure
points.brief: A gene has a promoter, exons that code and introns that are removed, and the genetic code reads in triplets.

points.title: Transcription
points.brief: RNA polymerase copies a gene's template strand into pre-mRNA in the nucleus.

points.title: RNA processing
points.brief: Pre-mRNA has introns removed, a cap and a poly-A tail added, making mature mRNA.

points.title: Translation
points.brief: Ribosomes read mRNA codons and tRNA brings matching amino acids, building a polypeptide.

points.title: Gene regulation and the trp operon
points.brief: In bacteria, the trp operon is switched off by a repressor when tryptophan is plentiful, saving energy.

points.title: Protein structure
points.brief: Amino acids join into polypeptides, which fold through four levels of structure into a working protein. All of an organism's proteins make its proteome.

points.title: The protein secretory pathway
points.brief: Proteins made on the rough ER move through the Golgi apparatus in vesicles and leave the cell by exocytosis.

points.title: Enzymes that manipulate DNA
points.brief: Endonucleases cut DNA, ligases join it and polymerases build it.

points.title: CRISPR-Cas9
points.brief: A bacterial defence adapted to edit genes, where a guide RNA leads Cas9 to cut DNA at a chosen place.

points.title: The polymerase chain reaction
points.brief: PCR copies DNA in cycles of denaturing, annealing primers and extending, making millions of copies.

points.title: Gel electrophoresis
points.brief: An electric field sorts DNA fragments by size through a gel, and the bands can be read for DNA profiling.

points.title: Recombinant plasmids
points.brief: A gene is cut and joined into a plasmid, which is put into bacteria by transformation so they make its product.

points.title: Genetically modified and transgenic organisms
points.brief: A GMO has altered DNA. A transgenic organism carries a gene from another species, such as pest-resistant crops.

points.title: Enzymes as catalysts
points.brief: Enzymes lower activation energy. The active site binds a matching substrate, as in the induced fit model.

points.title: Factors affecting enzymes
points.brief: Temperature, pH, and substrate and enzyme concentration change the rate of enzyme reactions.

points.title: Enzyme inhibition
points.brief: Competitive inhibitors block the active site. Non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and change its shape.

points.title: Coenzymes
points.brief: Molecules such as ATP, NADH and NADPH carry energy, electrons or hydrogen between reactions.

points.title: Photosynthesis overview
points.brief: In chloroplasts, light energy turns carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.

points.title: Light-dependent and light-independent stages
points.brief: The light-dependent stage in the thylakoids makes ATP and NADPH; the Calvin cycle in the stroma uses them to fix carbon.

points.title: C3, C4 and CAM plants
points.brief: C4 and CAM plants avoid wasteful reactions of Rubisco in hot, dry conditions by separating steps in space or time.

points.title: Factors affecting photosynthesis
points.brief: Light, carbon dioxide, temperature and water availability set the rate of photosynthesis.

points.title: Improving crop yields
points.brief: CRISPR-Cas9 could edit plants to photosynthesise more efficiently, for example by improving Rubisco, to raise crop yields.

points.title: Aerobic cellular respiration
points.brief: Glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain release energy from glucose, making about 30 to 32 ATP.

points.title: Anaerobic respiration
points.brief: Without oxygen, cells make only 2 ATP per glucose, producing lactic acid in animals or ethanol and carbon dioxide in yeast.

points.title: Factors affecting respiration
points.brief: Temperature, glucose and oxygen supply change the rate of cellular respiration.

points.title: Biofuels from fermentation
points.brief: Microbes ferment plant material anaerobically to make biofuels such as ethanol.

units.title: Unit 4: How does life change and respond to challenges?

points.title: Pathogens and antigens
points.brief: Antigens mark cells as self or non-self. Pathogens can be cellular, such as bacteria, or non-cellular, such as viruses. Allergens trigger responses too.

points.title: Physical, chemical and microbiological barriers
points.brief: Skin, mucus, stomach acid, enzymes and normal bacteria stop most pathogens getting in.

points.title: Barriers in plants
points.brief: Plants defend with thick cell walls, waxy cuticles and chemicals that harm pathogens.

points.title: The innate immune response
points.brief: A fast, non-specific response with inflammation, phagocytes, natural killer cells and complement proteins.

points.title: The lymphatic system
points.brief: Lymph nodes trap antigens and are where B and T cells meet them, starting the adaptive response.

points.title: Humoral immunity
points.brief: B cells make antibodies that bind antigens outside cells, neutralising them or marking them for destruction.

points.title: Cell-mediated immunity
points.brief: Helper T cells coordinate the response and cytotoxic T cells destroy infected or abnormal cells.

points.title: Immunological memory
points.brief: Memory B and T cells let the body respond faster and stronger to an antigen met before.

points.title: Natural and artificial immunity
points.brief: Active immunity comes from making your own antibodies, by infection or vaccination. Passive immunity comes from receiving antibodies.

points.title: Emerging and re-emerging diseases
points.brief: New pathogens emerge and old ones return in a connected world. Diseases brought by Europeans devastated Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.

points.title: Controlling the spread of disease
points.brief: Identifying the pathogen, its host and how it spreads lets scientists and communities control it with quarantine, hygiene and treatment.

points.title: Vaccination and herd immunity
points.brief: When enough people are vaccinated, a disease cannot spread easily, protecting those who cannot be vaccinated.

points.title: Monoclonal antibodies
points.brief: Antibodies made in the lab to target one antigen, used to treat cancers and autoimmune diseases.

points.title: Mutations
points.brief: Point mutations and changes to chromosomes create new alleles, the raw material for evolution.

points.title: The gene pool
points.brief: All the alleles in a population. Evolution is a change in allele frequencies over time.

points.title: Natural selection
points.brief: Individuals with traits suited to the environment survive and reproduce more, so their alleles become more common.

points.title: Genetic drift
points.brief: Chance changes in allele frequency, strongest in small populations, as in the bottleneck and founder effects.

points.title: Gene flow
points.brief: Movement of alleles between populations when individuals migrate and breed.

points.title: Selective breeding
points.brief: Humans choose which organisms breed, changing allele frequencies and reducing genetic diversity.

points.title: Antibiotic resistance
points.brief: Antibiotics kill susceptible bacteria and leave resistant ones to multiply, a case of natural selection.

points.title: Antigenic drift and shift
points.brief: Small changes (drift) and sudden big changes (shift) in viral antigens mean vaccines such as the flu vaccine must keep changing.

points.title: The fossil record
points.brief: Fossils show change over time through faunal succession, index fossils that date rock layers, and transitional fossils between groups.

points.title: Relative and absolute dating
points.brief: Relative dating orders fossils by rock layers and index fossils. Absolute dating gives an age from radioactive decay.

points.title: Speciation
points.brief: Isolated populations diverge into new species: Galapagos finches split by distance (allopatric), Lord Howe Island palms in one place (sympatric).

points.title: Comparative anatomy
points.brief: Homologous structures share an origin; vestigial structures have lost their use. Both show relatedness.

points.title: Molecular evidence
points.brief: Comparing DNA and amino acid sequences shows how closely species are related.

points.title: Phylogenetic trees
points.brief: Branching diagrams showing evolutionary relationships, with shared ancestors at each branch point.

points.title: Mammals, primates and hominins
points.brief: Shared features define mammals, primates, hominoids and hominins, placing humans in each group.

points.title: Human evolution
points.brief: From Australopithecus to Homo, hominins show larger brains and limbs suited to walking upright.

points.title: A contested fossil record
points.brief: New finds keep challenging how hominin fossils are classified, so the human family tree is refined or replaced.

points.title: Human migration
points.brief: Fossil and DNA evidence, such as mitochondrial DNA, traces modern humans around the world, including the arrival of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples' ancestors.

points.title: Variables and controlled experiments in biology
points.brief: Changing one independent variable, measuring the dependent variable and controlling the rest shows cause and effect.

points.title: Evidence for and against a hypothesis
points.brief: Data can support or refute a hypothesis, model or theory, and its sources of error and uncertainty limit how far.

points.title: Presenting a biology poster
points.brief: A scientific poster states an investigation briefly with correct terms and units, and acknowledges its sources.
